newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Manila painting campaign against drugs stirs row.
newsitem.headline: Manila painting campaign against drugs stirs row.

text.p: Human rights officials on Tuesday urged the Philippine Supreme Court to bar Manila's mayor from painting houses of alleged drug pushers with "Get out" signs, calling it cruel and degrading.
A resident of one of the more than 200 houses that have been painted joined the calls, saying he was not a drug pusher and had been falsely accused.

"We need your help to protect us from any future harassment ... We have no one to turn to," said a letter to the court by Daniel Saligumba, resident of one of the homes painted with slogans telling their occupants to leave the city.

Mayor Alfredo Lim sparked the uproar when he ordered police to spray-paint the doors of houses of alleged drug pushers and addicts with signs such as, "Beware, drug pusher's house", "Get out", and "Drug pusher lives here."
Many of the houses were those of slum-dwellers while one was home to a police officer accused of protecting drug traffickers.
Lim has said he welcomes challenges to his unorthodox campaign which, he says, is intended to stamp out the menace of drugs in the capital.
The mayor has earned the label "Dirty Harry" - after a trigger-happy Hollywood detective played by Clint Eastwood - for his methods in dealing with criminals.
Nasser Marohomsalic and Mercedes Contreras of the Philippine Commission on Human rights, along with Saligumba and several lawyers, asked the Supreme Court to declare Lim's campaign unconstitutional.

They said Lim's actions "degrade the dignity and integrity of those whose houses are spray-painted in that they immediately condemn said owners and occupants...as drug pushers without the benefit of a public trial."
The Supreme Court is to debate the petition next week.
